decks.title: File Handling — Part 1: Files, Paths and Text Files
goals: Tell text, binary and CSV files apart, and absolute paths from relative ones
Open files in the right mode, and close them, or use a with block
Read and write text files and move the file pointer with seek and tell
Write programs that count, search and copy lines of a text file

slides.heading: File Handling
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **files**, **paths**, **modes** and **text files**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why files, the three kinds of file, paths, open and modes, writing, reading, seek and tell, and processing lines
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: So far our programs forgot everything the moment they stopped. In this chapter we learn to keep data in files, so that it is still there tomorrow. In this first part we meet the three kinds of file, see how a program finds a file through its path, and learn to read and write text files.

slides.heading: Why do we need files?
slides.body_md: Data in variables live in **memory** and disappear when the program ends. A **file** keeps them on disk.

rows: Belong to one run of one program
Can be read later or by other programs
Stored on disk; can be very large

visual.alt: Comparison table: variables in memory are lost when a program ends and belong to one run, while data in a file persist, can be shared and can be large

slides.narration: Variables live in the computer memory, which is cleared when a program finishes. A file is stored on the disk, so its data persist after the program ends, can be read again later, and can be shared with other programs. That is why marks, bills and records are kept in files.

slides.heading: Three kinds of file

rows: Raw bytes, e.g. pickled Python objects
Records kept as lists or dictionaries

visual.alt: Table of the three kinds of file: text files store characters in lines, binary files store raw bytes such as pickled objects, and CSV files store comma-separated values; each with a typical use and how it is read

slides.narration: The syllabus covers three kinds of file. A text file holds characters arranged in lines, each ending with a newline character. A binary file holds raw bytes; we will use it to store Python lists and dictionaries with the pickle module. A CSV file is a text file in which each line is a record and the values are separated by commas.

slides.heading: Absolute and relative paths
slides.body_md: A **path** tells Python where a file is.

rows: Full location from the drive root
In the data folder inside the current one
In the parent of the current folder

visual.alt: Table of paths: two absolute paths, one for Windows starting with C drive and one for Linux starting with slash, and three relative paths for the current folder, a sub-folder and the parent folder
visual.caption: In a Python string write Windows paths as r"C:\School" or with doubled backslashes.

slides.narration: An absolute path gives the full address of a file, starting from the root of the drive, such as C drive on Windows or the slash folder on Linux. A relative path starts from the folder the program is running in, called the current working directory. Two dots stand for the parent folder. Most school programs use simple relative names like notes dot t x t.

slides.narration: Think about what write mode does when the file is missing, and what it does when the file already exists.

slides.heading: open() and file modes
slides.body_md:
```python
f = open("notes.txt", "a")
```

The **mode** decides what you may do and where the file pointer starts.

rows: Kept; writes go at the end

visual.alt: Table of file modes r, w, a, r plus, w plus and a plus, with what each opens for, what happens if the file exists or not, and where the file pointer starts; adding b gives the binary versions

slides.narration: The open function takes a file name and a mode, and returns a file object. Read mode is the default and needs the file to exist. Write mode creates the file or empties it. Append mode keeps old data and writes at the end. A plus sign adds the other operation, and the letter b gives the binary version of each mode.

slides.heading: Open, process, close and the with statement
slides.body_md:
```python
with open("notes.txt") as f:
    data = f.read()
# the file is closed here
```

nodes.label: open(name, mode) gives a file object
read or write through the object
close() saves and releases the file

visual.alt: Flow of file handling: open with a name and mode to get a file object, read or write through it, then close it to save and release the file
visual.caption: A with block does the close() for you.

slides.narration: Every file task has three steps: open the file, read or write through the file object, and close it. Closing saves the data and releases the file. A with block does the closing for us when the block ends, even if an error interrupts it, so it is the safest way to work with files.

slides.heading: Writing: write() and writelines()
slides.body_md:
```python
with open("demo.txt", "w") as f:
    n = f.write("Line one\n")
    f.writelines(["Line two\n", "Line three\n"])
print(n)
with open("demo.txt") as f:
    print(f.read(), end="")
```

rows: writes one string and returns its length: n is `9`
writes each string of the list, adding nothing between them

visual.alt: Table of writing methods run in Python: write returns the number of characters written, here 9, and writelines writes each string of a list; the file then holds three lines
visual.caption: Neither method adds a newline: put \n in the strings yourself.

slides.narration: The write method writes one string and returns the number of characters written. The writelines method writes every string in a list, one after another. Neither of them adds a newline on its own, so we must put the newline character at the end of each line ourselves. Writing a number directly is an error; convert it with str first.

slides.heading: Reading: read(), readline() and readlines()
slides.body_md:
The file `hills.txt`:

```text
Clouds gather over the hills
the bus waits at the stop
tea stalls open one by one
Evening lights come on
```

headers: Call on a freshly opened hills.txt
rows: `'Clouds gather over the hills\nthe bus waits at the stop\ntea stalls o`

visual.alt: Table of reading methods on a freshly opened hills.txt, run in Python: read gives the whole file as one string, read with 6 gives the first six characters, readline gives the first line with its newline, and readlines gives a list whose item 1 is the second line
visual.caption: read() returns one string; readline() one line; readlines() a list of lines (shown cut at 70 characters).

slides.narration: There are three ways to read a text file. The read method returns the whole remaining file as one string, or only a given number of characters. The readline method returns one line including its newline, and an empty string at the end of the file. The readlines method returns a list of all the remaining lines. A for loop over the file object also gives one line at a time.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting lines, words and characters
slides.body_md:
```python
lines = words = chars = 0
with open("hills.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        lines += 1
        words += len(line.split())
        chars += len(line)
print(lines, words, chars)
```

visual.alt: Trace table for counting lines, words and characters of hills.txt, run in Python: after 4 lines there are 21 words and 105 characters including the newlines
visual.caption: Dry run produced by running the loop in Python.

slides.narration: Let us count the lines, words and characters of hills dot t x t. The loop reads one line at a time. Each pass adds one to the line count, adds the number of words found by split, and adds the length of the line, which includes its newline character. The trace table shows the totals growing line by line.

slides.narration: Python keeps a file pointer that marks where the next read or write will happen. When a file is opened for reading, the pointer is at position zero. rows: `TypeError: write() argument must be str, not int`

visual.alt: Table of three common file errors produced by running Python: opening a missing file for reading, writing to a file opened for reading, and writing a number instead of a string

slides.narration: Three errors appear again and again. Opening a missing file for reading raises a file not found error. Writing to a file opened in read mode is not supported. And write accepts only strings, so writing a number raises a type error. Read the last line of the error message: it names the problem.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: absolute from the root; relative from the current folder
`r` must exist; `w` empties; `a` adds at the end

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: kinds of file, absolute and relative paths, the r, w and a modes, the with statement, the reading and writing methods, and tell and seek

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1: text files hold lines, binary files hold bytes and CSV files hold comma-separated text. Read mode needs an existing file, write mode empties it and append mode adds at the end. A with block closes the file for you. Use read, readline and readlines to read, write and writelines to write, and tell and seek for the pointer.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Choose the mode carefully: `w` **erases** an existing file; use `a` to add.
Output questions: track the **file pointer** after every `read(n)`, `readline()` and `seek()`.
Remember that lines keep their `\n`: use `strip()` before comparing or printing.
In programs, always open with `with` (or call `close()`), and convert numbers with `str()` before `write()`.
Marks: 1 for opening in the right mode, 1 for the loop, 1 for the logic, and the rest for correct output.
slides.narration: Some advice for the exam. Choose the mode with care, because write mode erases an existing file. In output questions, follow the file pointer after every read and seek. Lines keep their newline characters, so strip them before comparing. In programs, use a with block and convert numbers to strings before writing. Marks are given for the mode, the loop, the logic and the output.

decks.title: File Handling — Part 2: Binary Files and CSV Files
goals: Store and read Python objects in binary files with pickle.dump() and pickle.load()
Read a binary file to the end by handling EOFError, and search and update its records
Write and read CSV files with csv.writer and csv.reader

slides.heading: Binary Files and CSV Files
slides.body_md: Part 2 — storing **Python objects** with pickle, and **tables** in CSV files.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: binary files and pickle, dump and load, reading until EOFError, searching and updating records, CSV files, the csv writer and the csv reader
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 2 we store data that has more structure than lines of text. First we use binary files and the pickle module to save whole Python lists and dictionaries, and read them back. Then we use CSV files, which store tables that both Python and spreadsheets understand.

slides.heading: Binary files and pickle
slides.body_md: A record such as `[101, "Desert Sky", 240]` can be stored **as it is** in a binary file.

visual.alt: Table of pickle terms: pickling or serialisation turns an object into bytes with dump, unpickling or deserialisation turns bytes back into an object with load, and binary modes such as wb, rb and ab are used

slides.narration: Writing a list to a text file would turn it into characters, and we would have to rebuild it ourselves. The pickle module does this for us. Pickling converts an object into a stream of bytes, which dump writes to a binary file. Unpickling, done by load, turns the bytes back into the same kind of object.

slides.heading: From object to bytes and back
slides.body_md:
```python
import pickle
with open("books.dat", "wb") as f:
    pickle.dump([101, "Desert Sky", 240], f)
    pickle.dump([102, "Paper Boats", 180], f)
with open("books.dat", "rb") as f:
    print(pickle.load(f))
    print(pickle.load(f)[1])
```

Output:

```text
[101, 'Desert Sky', 240]
Paper Boats
```

nodes.label: The same list or dictionary again

visual.alt: Flow of pickling: a Python list or dictionary is written as bytes by dump into a binary file, and load reads the bytes back into an equal list or dictionary
visual.caption: Each dump() writes one object; each load() reads the next one.

slides.narration: Here two book records are dumped one after the other into books dot dat, opened in write binary mode. Reading in read binary mode, each call to load returns the next record in the order it was written. The first load gives the whole first list; the second gives the second list, from which we print the title.

slides.heading: A file of records
slides.body_md:
The imagined file `books.dat` holds four records:

```text
[101, "Desert Sky", 240]
[102, "Paper Boats", 180]
[103, "Hill Station Tales", 320]
[104, "Lantern Lane", 150]
```

visual.alt: Table of the four imagined book records stored in books.dat, each as a list of book id, title and price: Desert Sky 240, Paper Boats 180, Hill Station Tales 320 and Lantern Lane 150
visual.caption: Imagined records; each list is written with one pickle.dump().

slides.narration: Most binary file programs work with a file of records, one pickled list or dictionary per record. In our examples, books dot dat holds four imagined books, each stored as a list of the book number, the title and the price. Programs search, count, add and update these records.

slides.heading: Reading to the end: EOFError

visual.alt: Flow of reading a binary file to the end: open in rb, inside try load and process records repeatedly, and stop when load raises EOFError
visual.caption: The EOFError is expected: it means every record has been read.

slides.narration: We usually do not know how many records a file holds. So we call load again and again in an endless loop inside a try block. When no record is left, load raises an end of file error, and the except clause quietly ends the loop. This pattern appears in almost every binary file question.

nodes.label: Load every record into a list ("rb")
Find the record and change it in the list

slides.heading: CSV files
slides.body_md:
The imagined file `marks.csv`:

```text
roll,name,marks
1,Aarav,78
2,Bina,91
3,Chetan,64
4,Divya,85
```

visual.alt: Table showing the first three lines of marks.csv as text, as spreadsheet cells, and as the lists of strings that csv reader returns when run in Python
visual.caption: Every field comes back as a string.

slides.narration: A CSV file is a text file in which each line is a record and its values are separated by commas. The first line is often a header naming the columns. Spreadsheets open CSV files as tables. In Python, the csv module reads each line as a list of strings, as the table shows.

slides.heading: Writing a CSV file

visual.alt: Table of the steps for writing a CSV file: import csv, open with newline equal to empty string, create a writer, write one row with writerow, write many with writerows, and close

slides.narration: To write a CSV file, import the csv module and open the file with newline set to an empty string. Create a writer object from the file. Then writerow writes one list as one line, and writerows writes a list of lists, one line each. Numbers are written as text. Finally close the file, or use a with block.

slides.heading: Reading a CSV file
slides.body_md:
```python
import csv
with open("marks.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.reader(f):
        print(row)
```

Output:

```text
['roll', 'name', 'marks']
['1', 'Aarav', '78']
['2', 'Bina', '91']
['3', 'Chetan', '64']
['4', 'Divya', '85']
```

visual.alt: Table of reading tasks: skip the header with next, convert numbers with int or float, and get all rows with list

slides.narration: A reader object gives one row at a time as a list of strings. The header comes first, so call next once to skip it. Because every field is a string, convert numbers with int or float before doing arithmetic. To keep all the rows, turn the reader into a list.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: average marks
slides.body_md:
```python
import csv
total = 0
with open("marks.csv", newline="") as f:
    r = csv.reader(f)
    next(r)
    for roll, name, m in r:
        total += int(m)
print(total / 4)
```

visual.caption: Dry run produced by running the loop in Python; the last row is the average.

slides.narration: To find the average mark, we open marks dot c s v, create a reader and skip the header. For each row we unpack roll, name and marks, convert the marks with int and add them to the total. The trace table, produced by running the program, shows the total growing and the average at the end.

sections.heading: 1. Files, kinds of file and paths
sections.body_md:
A **file** keeps data on disk after a program ends (data in variables are lost).

- **Text file:** characters in lines; each line ends with the EOL character `\n`. Readable in any editor.
- **Binary file:** raw bytes, e.g. Python objects stored with **pickle**; not human-readable.
- **CSV file:** a text file of **comma-separated values**, one record per line; opens in spreadsheets.

**Paths.** An **absolute path** starts at the root (`C:\School\cs\a.txt`, `/home/asha/cs/a.txt`). A **relative path** starts at the **current working directory** (`a.txt`, `data\a.txt`, `..\a.txt`, where `..` is the parent folder).

sections.heading: 2. Opening and closing files
sections.body_md:
`f = open(name, mode)` returns a **file object**; `f.close()` saves and releases the file.

- `"r"` read (default; file must exist), `"w"` write (creates or **empties**), `"a"` append (creates or adds at the end).
- `"r+"`, `"w+"`, `"a+"` add the other operation; add `b` for binary: `"rb"`, `"wb"`, `"ab"`.

The **with statement** closes the file automatically, even after an error:

```python
with open("notes.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("New entry\n")
```

**Reading:** `read()` → whole remaining text as one string; `read(n)` → n characters; `readline()` → one line (`""` at the end of the file); `readlines()` → list of lines; `for line in f:` → one line per pass.

sections.heading: 5. Binary files with pickle
sections.body_md:
`import pickle`. **Pickling** (`pickle.dump(obj, f)`) writes an object as bytes; **unpickling** (`pickle.load(f)`) reads the next object back.

- Open in `"wb"` (new file), `"ab"` (add records) or `"rb"` (read).
- **Read till the end:** call `load()` in `while True` inside `try`, and stop on `except EOFError`.
- **Search:** load each record and test it; use a flag to report "not found".
- **Update:** load all records into a list, change in memory, dump all again in `"wb"`.

Appending a fifth record and counting again (run in Python):

```python
import pickle
with open("books.dat", "ab") as f:
    pickle.dump([105, "Blue Kettle", 210], f)
n = 0
with open("books.dat", "rb") as f:
    try:
        while True:
            pickle.load(f)
            n += 1
    except EOFError:
        pass
print(n)
```

Output: `5`

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A text file stores characters with an end-of-line marker; a binary file stores bytes exactly as they are in memory. Text files hold human-readable characters, organised into lines that end with an EOL character. Binary files hold raw bytes (for example pickled Python objects), which look like junk in a text editor. Extensions are only conventions.

questions.stem_md: What is the **default delimiter** that separates values in a CSV file?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A comma. CSV stands for comma-separated values. Each record is one line, and its fields are separated by commas by default; another delimiter can be chosen with the delimiter argument.

questions.stem_md: Kavya keeps her project at `D:\Class12\Project`. Which of these is an **absolute** path to the file `scores.txt` inside its `data` folder?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** `D:\Class12\Project\data\scores.txt`. An absolute path starts from the root of the drive (D:\) and names every folder on the way. The other three are relative paths, worked out from the current working directory.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** `/home/ravi/school/maths/sums.txt`. Two dots mean the parent of the current folder, here /home/ravi/school. From there the path goes into maths and names sums.txt.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A file written with the `pickle` module usually shows unreadable symbols when opened in a plain text editor.
questions.solution_md: **True.** pickle writes a binary encoding of Python objects, not lines of characters, so a text editor shows symbols that do not make sense to a reader.

questions.stem_md: A school wants to store (a) the text of its daily notices, (b) student records as Python dictionaries to be searched and updated by a program, and (c) a marks table that teachers will also open in a spreadsheet. questions.solution_md: Three choices with reasons and a comparison of the three kinds of file.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **(a) Text file:** notices are characters in lines; anyone can read or edit them in a text editor.
2. **(b) Binary file with pickle:** dictionaries are dumped and loaded **as Python objects**, with no conversion to strings; the data are not readable by people, which also discourages casual editing.
3. **(c) CSV file:** a CSV file is plain text with comma-separated fields, so **spreadsheets** and the **csv module** can both use it.
4. **Text and CSV** files store everything as characters, so numbers must be converted with int() after reading; **binary** files keep the types.
5. Reading: text files with read()/readline(); binary files with **load() until EOFError**; CSV files with **csv.reader**.
